subject: English Literature
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature (4ET1)
source: Edexcel spec: content/syllabus/ks4/english-literature.json (4ET1, Issue 3), units 2A, 2A-OPT, 2B, 2B-OPT and 2B-SCH, written from own knowledge; no Drive material was used. Macbeth (public domain, school choice) taught for Component 2/3 Section B; the earlier AQA 8702 Macbeth lessons were retired (30 marks, AO1, AO2, AO4, open book); extracts are at most 3 lines, cited by act.scene (numbering varies slightly by edition). Drama lessons are option-neutral methods with models from An Inspector Calls; the other four plays appear in a context table only. The school's choice of play and of Component 2 versus Component 3 is undecided.

lessons.title: Modern drama: reading a play as performance (stage directions and dramatic methods)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do playwrights use the stage, not just the words, to shape what an audience feels?
objectives: Explain how stage directions, lighting and entrances create meaning
Analyse dramatic irony and structure in a play
Write an analytical point about a dramatic method
successCriteria: All: identify a stage direction and say what it shows
Most: analyse a dramatic method with its effect on the audience
Some: link a method to the playwright's purpose and context
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama: staging and performance; History: Britain in 1912 and 1945
lessons.smsc: Moral: social responsibility and collective duty

keywords.def: the playwright's instructions about setting, movement, sound and lighting
when the audience knows something a character does not
when a character comes on stage
the build-up of suspense or conflict
a technique specific to drama, such as staging or dialogue

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between a novel and a play as a form?
Name three things a stage direction can tell you.
Define 'audience response'.

teach.heading: Drama is written to be performed
bullets: Words, silence, movement and sound all create meaning
AO2: analyse how the playwright shapes meaning
Refer to the audience, not the 'reader'
Component 2 is open book: you can use your play
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain Component 2 Section A (30 marks, one question from two, AO1 and AO2; Component 3 is the coursework alternative). TEACHER: the school must choose one play from the list: A View from the Bridge, An Inspector Calls, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time (the Simon Stephens adaptation), Kindertransport, Death and the King's Horseman. Supply class copies. The models below use An Inspector Calls (Priestley, written 1945, set 1912); adapt them to your chosen text.

teach.heading: Model: staging as meaning
teach.note: I do. The stage direction at the Inspector's arrival says the lighting changes from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder' and describes him as creating an impression of 'massiveness, solidity and purposefulness'. Check these phrases against the class edition before the lesson. Show how the paragraph analyses what the audience sees and hears, not what a reader imagines.

model.problem: How does Priestley use stage directions to present the Inspector's arrival?
steps: Point: the lighting change signals a shift from comfort to scrutiny.
Evidence: the lighting turns from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder'.
Zoom: the soft colour of the first suggests a cosy, private party, while 'harder' suggests exposure, as if the family are under interrogation.
Link: his 'massiveness, solidity and purposefulness' gives an authority that disturbs the Birlings' complacency.
model.answer: Priestley uses lighting to signal a shift from comfort to scrutiny. The 'pink and intimate' light suggests a cosy, private celebration, but the change to 'brighter and harder' makes the stage feel like an interrogation room, exposing the family. The Inspector's 'massiveness, solidity and purposefulness' adds an authority that disturbs the Birlings' complacency, and the audience sees the mood change at once.

teach.heading: Dramatic irony in the audience's seat
teach.note: Use the compare block to show how irony works. In Act 1, Mr Birling confidently says the Titanic is 'unsinkable' and that there will be no war; the 1945 audience knows both are wrong. Explain it as a way of discrediting Birling and his views. The same method can be found in each set play: ask pupils to hunt for what the audience knows that the characters do not.

left.title: What the character says
points: Believes that each man must look after himself

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils often write about 'the writer says' with no sense of performance. Prompt them: what does the audience see, hear and feel? B is correct; D describes plot only.

check.q: Which sentence is the best analysis of dramatic method?
options: The Inspector enters in Act 1.
The sudden hardening of the lighting makes the audience feel exposed alongside the Birlings.
Priestley wrote the play in 1945.
The Birlings are rich.
check.why: B names a method and explains the audience's experience. A and D describe plot; C is a context fact without link.

teach.heading: Structure of a play
bullets: Acts and scenes build and release tension
Cliffhangers end acts
Entrances and exits shift power
The final moments leave the audience with a question
teach.note: Ask pupils to map their play's structure on one line: beginning, turning point, climax, ending. In An Inspector Calls, the closing phone call reveals that a real inspector is on his way, leaving the audience unsettled; similar structural choices occur in other plays. Remind them that AO2 includes structure: comment on why a scene comes where it does.

practice: Why might a playwright end an act on a revelation?
What is the difference between 'character' and 'role'?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on one stage direction in your play.
Extend: write a paragraph on the effect of dramatic irony.
Stretch: write a paragraph on how the structure of the play shapes the audience's sympathy.
exit: What does a stage direction tell us?
Name one dramatic method and its effect.
Big question: how do playwrights use the stage to shape what an audience feels?
lessons.homework: Choose a short scene from your play and write a 150-word paragraph on one dramatic method.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach theatre vocabulary with images of a stage plan. Offer a paragraph frame. Stretch: sketch the staging of one scene and explain the choices.

lessons.title: Modern drama: the open-book response (AO1 and AO2) and context in the options
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an open-book exam help you write a more precise, sophisticated answer?
objectives: Select short, precise evidence from the play in an open-book setting
Write an answer that covers whole-play structure and key moments
Use context sparingly and relevantly
successCriteria: All: find and use two short quotations
Most: write two paragraphs on a theme or character
Some: link early and late scenes in one paragraph
lessons.crossCurricular: History: context of each play; Drama: performance

keywords.def: an exam where you may use your copy of the text
mark a key page for quick access
using ideas from across the play's beginning, middle and end
choosing only the words that matter
actions and movements that add meaning

starter: Bismillah. What is dramatic irony?
Name a theme in your play and one moment that shows it.
Why is a long quotation less useful than a short one?

teach.heading: Open book does not mean less thinking
bullets: Mark your five key moments before the exam
Quote briefly and analyse deeply
Examiners credit the choice of evidence
Coursework (Component 3) also allows time to draft
teach.note: TEACHER: check the school's entry decision (Component 2 or 3) with the exams officer. Explain that a bulky book can slow candidates down: advise pupils to tab five moments (opening, a turning point, a climax, a revelation, the ending) and to annotate with technique labels. In Component 2 Section A, check the latest past papers for question wording and whether extracts are printed.

teach.heading: Options: what to know for each play
teach.note: Use as a revision guide, not as a lecture. Confirm facts in class copies and in reliable references. Ask pupils to add a column for two dramatic methods and one key moment in their chosen play.

teach.heading: Model: a whole-play paragraph
teach.note: I do. This model uses An Inspector Calls; adapt it. Show how the paragraph links the start and end of the play, which is a mark of sophistication. Check that pupils see the quotation is short and integrated.

model.problem: Explore how Priestley presents Mr Birling in the play.
steps: Point: Priestley presents Birling as complacent and wrong, from the start to the end.
Evidence: at the dinner he calls the Titanic 'unsinkable'; at the end he worries more about scandal than about the girl.
Zoom: the early dramatic irony mocks his predictions, and the later reaction shows he has not learned.
Context: Priestley wrote in 1945 to argue for shared social responsibility after the war.
model.answer: Priestley presents Mr Birling as complacent and wrong throughout. At the start, his confident claim that the Titanic is 'unsinkable' invites the audience to mock his predictions, which dramatic irony reveals to be false. By the end, his concern is for scandal rather than for the girl, so the audience sees that he has learned nothing, while Priestley's 1945 audience would see in him the attitudes that the postwar world needed to reject.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils may choose D because it sounds impressive. Explain that only B shows the sophistication of covering start and end with precise evidence.

check.q: Which approach is best for an open-book answer?
options: Copy out long passages to show you know the play.
Use short quotations from the start and the end and analyse a word in each.
Retell the plot in order.
Avoid quotations and speak generally.
check.why: B shows precision and a whole-play view. A wastes time, C is narrative, D gives no evidence.

teach.heading: Timing and planning
bullets: Choose one of two questions: 3 minutes
Plan: 7 minutes
Write: 35 minutes
Check: 5 minutes
teach.note: The paper is 1 hour 30 minutes for two 30-mark questions, so about 45 minutes each. The timings are a guide: check the latest advice. Practise using the tabs and a short plan. Pupils time themselves writing one planned paragraph.

practice: Why might context be best placed inside analysis rather than at the start?
independent: Core: tab five moments in your play and write a technique label for each.
Extend: write a paragraph linking two moments.
Stretch: write a paragraph that uses context to explain a dramatic choice.
exit: Name one tabbed moment and why it matters.
Write one integrated quotation.
Big question: how can an open-book exam help you write a precise answer?
lessons.homework: Write a plan and one paragraph for an original question: 'Explore how the playwright presents responsibility (or loyalty) in your set play.'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pre-tabbed layout and a sentence-starter bank. Extra reading time if agreed. Stretch: write the opening and closing paragraphs of a full answer.

lessons.title: Macbeth: Jacobean context, the exam and the world of the play
lessons.bigQuestion: Why did Shakespeare's audience fear what Macbeth does?
objectives: Explain James I's reign, the Gunpowder Plot and divine right as context
Understand how Component 2 Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4
Link a context point to a short quotation
successCriteria: All: state two Jacobean beliefs
Most: link one belief to a moment in the play
Some: explain how context shapes Shakespeare's choices
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Jacobean England, James I and the Gunpowder Plot
lessons.smsc: Moral: the cost of unlawful ambition; Spiritual: accountability and the consequences of wrongdoing

keywords.def: the killing of a king
the belief that a monarch is appointed by God
from the reign of James I (1603-1625)
speaking in a misleading way while claiming not to lie
a play in which a great person falls through a flaw and choices

starter: Bismillah. What is context? Give one example from a text you know.
Which AOs does the literary heritage question assess?
Define 'tragic hero'.

teach.heading: Macbeth in the exam
bullets: Component 2 Section B: one 30-mark question from two
AO1, AO2 and AO4; open book
Component 3 route: a coursework assignment
Macbeth is on the Pearson list
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that Macbeth is on the Pearson list of literary heritage options, so it is valid for this course. In Component 2 the text is open book, so quotation recall matters less than choosing and analysing evidence. Check the prescribed edition and line numbers: act.scene references in these lessons may differ by a line or two between editions. TEACHER: supply class copies of Macbeth.

teach.heading: Jacobean timeline
teach.note: Walk through the dates and ask: which event would most influence a playwright? Remind pupils that historians differ on the exact date of the play, so say 'probably written around 1606'. Link to James I's fascination with witchcraft (Daemonologie) and his fear of plots.

timeline.text: James VI of Scotland publishes Daemonologie on witchcraft
He becomes James I of England; Shakespeare's company becomes the King's Men
The Gunpowder Plot: a failed plot to blow up Parliament and the king

teach.heading: Beliefs that shape the play
bullets: Divine right: the king is God's deputy
Regicide is the worst of crimes
Disorder in the state and in nature go together
Witchcraft is feared as real
teach.note: Explain divine right: a king was thought to be chosen by God, so killing one was a sin against heaven as well as the state. Explain the Great Chain of Being briefly: a ranked order from God to angels to kings to people to animals, which a murder of a king disrupts. Be careful: do not claim all Jacobeans believed the same thing; say 'many people believed'. Ask: how might an audience who had just lived through the Gunpowder Plot respond to the murder of Duncan?

teach.heading: Model: linking context and quotation
teach.note: I do. Use a short extract and integrate it. Cite act.scene exactly. Show how the paragraph does not begin with context; context supports the analysis.

model.problem: Explore how Shakespeare presents the supernatural in Macbeth.
steps: Point: Shakespeare opens the play in a disordered, supernatural world.
Evidence: the witches' chant that 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' (1.1).
Zoom: the paradox reverses moral values and unsettles the audience from the first scene; the rhythm of a spell adds menace.
Context: James I believed in witchcraft, so many in the audience would take the witches as a real threat.
model.answer: Shakespeare opens the play in a disordered, supernatural world. The witches' paradox 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' (1.1) reverses moral values and unsettles the audience at once, while the chant-like rhythm adds menace. Because James I wrote about witchcraft and many in the audience feared it, the witches would seem a real threat, not a fairy tale.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: B is the best answer. A and D are bolt-ons; C is the text but no link.

options: James I was king in 1606.
Because the Gunpowder Plot had threatened the king's life, the murder of Duncan would have horrified an audience.
Macbeth is a play about a Scottish king.
Many people liked plays.
check.why: B links an event to the audience's response. A and D are facts without link; C is plot.

teach.heading: Quote: the first words of the play
teach.note: Read the extract aloud. Ask pupils to annotate for sound, paradox and mood. This is the first of the extracts they will annotate across the unit. Cite 1.1 in their notes. A common line is 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair'; line numbers vary slightly by edition.

quote.text:
Fair is foul, and foul is fair:
Hover through the fog and filthy air.

practice: Retrieve: what is the difference between AO2 and AO4?
Name two features of a tragedy.
independent: Core: write a paragraph linking one Jacobean belief to a moment in 1.1.
Extend: write a paragraph about the witches and James I.
Stretch: evaluate how far context explains the play's horror of regicide.
exit: Name two Jacobean beliefs.
Write one sentence linking context to a quotation.
Big question: why did Shakespeare's audience fear what Macbeth does?
lessons.homework: Read Act 1, scenes 1 to 3 and note three short quotations about the witches or Macbeth.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a one-page Jacobean fact sheet and a glossary. Use a short modern-English summary of each scene alongside the text. Stretch: research how historians date the play.

lessons.title: Macbeth Act 1: the witches, the prophecy and ambition
lessons.bigQuestion: Is Macbeth tempted or does he choose?
objectives: Analyse how Shakespeare presents Macbeth in Act 1
Explain the effect of the witches' prophecy
Use a short extract to build a paragraph on ambition
successCriteria: All: summarise Macbeth's first reactions
Most: analyse a short quotation about ambition
Some: debate temptation versus choice
lessons.crossCurricular: History: kingship and succession; PSHE: responsibility for choices
lessons.smsc: Moral: temptation and free will; Spiritual: accountability for our decisions

keywords.def: a strong desire to achieve power or success
a prediction about the future
words spoken to the audience, not the other characters
a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone
the flaw that leads to a tragic hero's fall

starter: Bismillah. Define 'soliloquy'.
Give two Jacobean beliefs about kings.
What does 'regicide' mean?

teach.heading: From hero to tempted man
bullets: In 1.2 Macbeth is a brave, loyal soldier
The witches meet him in 1.3 and hail him as king to be
He is startled and afraid
Banquo is suspicious, Macbeth is intrigued
teach.note: Summarise 1.2 and 1.3 and ask: what does the audience think of Macbeth before he meets the witches? Likely answer: a brave, loyal hero ('brave Macbeth'). After the witches, his first reaction is fear and fascination. Note the contrast with Banquo, who warns that the 'instruments of darkness tell us truths, / Win us with honest trifles, to betray's'. Cite 1.3 and say that the exact line numbers vary.

teach.heading: Macbeth's asides
teach.note: Read the extract aloud. Pupils annotate the conditional 'If' and the verb 'crown'. Ask: does he sound like a man who will act, or a man who will wait? Explain that an aside lets the audience see what the other characters cannot: a clue that Macbeth's mind is secretly changing.

quote.text:
If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me
Without my stir.

teach.heading: Model: ambition in Act 1
teach.note: I do. The model uses the soliloquy in 1.7, short extract: 'I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself / And falls on th' other.' Explain the image of a horseman who leaps too high and falls. Show how the paragraph analyses imagery and structure.

model.problem: Explore how Shakespeare presents ambition in Act 1.
steps: Point: Macbeth recognises that his ambition is dangerous.
Evidence: he admits his only 'spur' is 'Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself' (1.7).
Zoom: the horse-riding image suggests ambition as a rider who overreaches and falls; the unfinished line 'And falls on th' other' mirrors a fall.
Link: that he still goes on shows ambition overcomes conscience.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents ambition as something Macbeth recognises and still cannot resist. He admits that his only 'spur' is 'Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself' (1.7), an image of a rider who jumps too far and falls, which suggests that he knows the danger. The broken line that follows ('And falls on th' other') mirrors the fall, and the fact that he continues shows that ambition overpowers his conscience.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss D, a common misconception that Macbeth is simply evil. Shakespeare presents him as a conflicted hero, which makes the tragedy more powerful.

check.q: What does the audience learn in the opening of the play about Macbeth?
options: He is a cruel tyrant.
He is admired as a brave soldier before he meets the witches.
He is a witch.
He wants to be a farmer.
check.why: B is correct: the contrast between his early reputation and his later actions is key to the tragedy. A is later; C and D are false.

teach.heading: Temptation or choice?
bullets: The witches predict but do not command
Macbeth chooses to act
Lady Macbeth will push him
Debate: who is more responsible?
teach.note: Run a class continuum debate: how much are the witches responsible? Ask pupils to use quotations from 1.3 and 1.7. Encourage a balanced view for the AO1 personal engagement. Link to a moral idea: in Islam, humans are accountable for their choices; keep the discussion focused on the text.

practice: Name two beliefs about witches in 1606.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the witches' effect in 1.1 and 1.3.
Extend: write a paragraph on Macbeth's soliloquy in 1.7.
Stretch: write a paragraph arguing who is more to blame: the witches or Macbeth.
exit: Name one quotation about ambition.
Is Macbeth tempted or does he choose? Give one reason.
Big question: is Macbeth tempted or does he choose?
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word paragraph exploring how Macbeth is presented before he meets the witches and afterwards.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a plain-language summary of 1.3 and 1.7 and highlight key words in the text. Stretch: read the play's sources (Holinshed) in extract and compare.

lessons.title: Macbeth Act 1: Lady Macbeth, Duncan and the decision to kill
lessons.bigQuestion: How does Lady Macbeth turn her husband's doubt into action?
objectives: Analyse Lady Macbeth's language in 1.5 and 1.7
Explain how Shakespeare presents Duncan
Discuss gender and power in the play
successCriteria: All: describe Lady Macbeth's plan
Most: analyse imagery and imperatives
Some: evaluate how far gender expectations shape the characters
lessons.crossCurricular: History: gender roles in Jacobean England; Drama: persuasive speech
lessons.smsc: Moral: manipulation and conscience; Social: the abuse of influence

keywords.def: a command
controlling someone by clever or unfair means
language that creates pictures
when the audience knows more than a character
qualities traditionally linked with women

starter: Bismillah. What is an imperative verb?
Name one moment of dramatic irony from Act 1.
What does 'o'erleaps' suggest?

teach.heading: Lady Macbeth enters
bullets: She reads Macbeth's letter in 1.5
She fears his nature is 'too full o' th' milk of human kindness'
She calls on spirits to 'unsex' her
She advises him to 'Look like th' innocent flower'
teach.note: Explain 1.5: Lady Macbeth reads a letter from her husband and at once plans. Ask pupils to find verbs of command. Context: in Jacobean England women were expected to be obedient and gentle, so her wish to be 'unsexed' would seem unnatural to many in the audience. Be careful to present this as a view of the time, not a judgement of today. Cite 1.5.

teach.heading: Imperatives and imagery
teach.note: Pupils annotate the extract for imperatives and the serpent image. Ask: what does this tell us about her plan, and about her view of appearances? Link to the theme of appearance and reality.

quote.text:
Look like th' innocent flower,
But be the serpent under't.

teach.heading: Model: Lady Macbeth's persuasion
teach.note: I do. The model is based on 1.7, where she mocks his courage: 'screw your courage to the sticking-place'. Explain the phrase (a screw tightened to hold a crossbow ready). Show how the paragraph analyses a word and a method.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth as persuasive in 1.7?
steps: Point: she persuades through commands and challenges to his manhood.
Evidence: she tells him to 'screw your courage to the sticking-place'.
Zoom: the imperative 'screw' is forceful and mechanical, treating courage as something you can tighten; the image makes failure sound weak.
Context: Jacobean ideas of masculinity add to the power of her challenge.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as persuasive through commands and challenges to Macbeth's manhood. Her imperative 'screw your courage to the sticking-place' is forceful and mechanical, as if courage were a thing to be tightened and fixed, and it suggests that hesitation is a weakness. Jacobean assumptions about manliness would give her challenge extra power.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: A is the misconception that Lady Macbeth is simply 'evil'. A fuller reading: she is persuasive and ambitious but later destroyed by guilt.

check.q: Which statement best sums up Lady Macbeth in Act 1?
options: She is kind and gentle.
She is determined and uses language to manipulate Macbeth into action.
She is afraid of the witches.
She is a witch.
check.why: B reflects her commands and challenges. A, C and D do not fit.

teach.heading: Duncan: a trusting king
bullets: He praises Macbeth and trusts him
He is the ideal gracious king
The audience knows he is in danger: dramatic irony
His murder breaks the natural order
teach.note: Show how Duncan's trust ('He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust', 1.4, about the traitorous Thane of Cawdor) is ironic because he soon trusts another traitor. The pleasant description of the castle in 1.6 adds irony. Ask: why does Shakespeare make Duncan so good? Likely answer: to make the crime worse and to increase our horror.

practice: Retrieve: define 'dramatic irony' and give one example.
Name three Jacobean ideas about kingship.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on 1.5 using the model.
Extend: write a paragraph on Duncan's trust and dramatic irony.
Stretch: write a paragraph on whether Lady Macbeth or Macbeth is more to blame for the decision to kill.
exit: Name one imperative from Lady Macbeth.
Why does Shakespeare make Duncan so good?
Big question: how does Lady Macbeth turn doubt into action?
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word paragraph on how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in 1.5.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a speech-by-speech summary and highlight imperatives in colour. Stretch: stage 1.7 in pairs and discuss how tone of voice changes the meaning.

lessons.title: Macbeth Acts 2 and 3: the dagger, guilt and the murder of Banquo
lessons.bigQuestion: How does guilt change Macbeth and Lady Macbeth?
objectives: Analyse the dagger soliloquy and the aftermath of the murder
Explain how Shakespeare presents guilt and the supernatural
Link blood imagery across Acts 2 and 3
successCriteria: All: summarise key events in 2.1-3.4
Most: analyse blood imagery
Some: trace the shift in the couple's relationship
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama: soliloquy and staging; Psychology: guilt and conscience
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: conscience, remorse and repentance (tawbah) as human ideas; Moral: the cost of wrongdoing

keywords.def: a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone
repeated references to blood as a symbol of guilt
seeing things that are not there
a repeated image or idea
a ruler who uses power cruelly

starter: Bismillah. What is a motif?
Give two reasons Macbeth kills Duncan.
What does Lady Macbeth say in 1.7 to persuade him?

teach.heading: The dagger
bullets: 2.1: Macbeth sees a dagger in the air
He cannot tell if it is real
The soliloquy shows his guilt before the act
The bell signals the murder
teach.note: Read the extract aloud twice. Ask pupils to annotate the question form and the contrast between 'see' and 'have'. Explain that on stage the dagger may or may not be shown; discuss the effect of each choice. Cite 2.1.

quote.text:
Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee.
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.

teach.heading: After the murder: blood
teach.note: In 2.2 Macbeth is horrified: he fears that the sea cannot wash his hands clean. Lady Macbeth is more practical: she says 'A little water clears us of this deed'. The contrast shows differing reactions. Later (5.1) her reaction will reverse. Use the compare block to draw out the contrast.

left.title: Macbeth (2.2)
points: 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?'
Hears a voice: 'Macbeth does murder sleep'

right.title: Lady Macbeth (2.2)
points: 'A little water clears us of this deed'
Scorns his fear and returns the daggers

teach.heading: Model: blood and guilt
teach.note: I do. Read the extract: 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather / The multitudinous seas incarnadine, / Making the green one red' (2.2). Explain 'incarnadine' as 'turn red'. Note the contrast of the huge sea with one hand.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's guilt in 2.2?
steps: Point: guilt is presented as overwhelming and permanent.
Evidence: his hand will turn 'The multitudinous seas incarnadine'.
Zoom: the polysyllabic 'multitudinous' and the huge image of the oceans turning red suggest a guilt so vast that nothing can cleanse it.
Link: Lady Macbeth's belief that 'a little water' will do shows how differently they respond, a difference that later reverses.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents Macbeth's guilt as overwhelming. His claim that his hand will turn 'The multitudinous seas incarnadine' uses a vast image, and the long, heavy word 'multitudinous' makes the guilt seem too large to wash away. In contrast, Lady Macbeth's belief that 'a little water' will do shows how differently they respond, a difference that will later reverse.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: A is the misconception that Macbeth has stopped feeling guilt. In 2.2 his guilt is immediate; by 3.4 where he says he is 'in blood / Stepped in so far' that turning back is as hard as going on.

check.q: What does 'I am in blood / Stepped in so far' (3.4) suggest?
options: He regrets nothing.
He feels trapped: going back is as difficult as going forward.
He is proud of his killing.
He is going to give up the crown.
check.why: B reflects the river image: he is committed to more bloodshed. A and C ignore the tone of trapped despair; D is not supported.

teach.heading: Banquo and the banquet
bullets: 3.1: Macbeth fears Banquo's descendants
He arranges Banquo's murder
3.4: Banquo's ghost appears at the feast
Lady Macbeth covers for him in front of the lords
teach.note: Explain that Macbeth says 'To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus' (3.1): a throne is worth nothing without security. In 3.4 the ghost is seen only by Macbeth: ask whether it is real or the product of guilt. Both readings are valid: encourage tentative language. Link to Jacobean belief in ghosts and to the idea that Banquo is an ancestor of James I.

practice: Why does Shakespeare place the murder offstage?
independent: Core: write a paragraph on the dagger soliloquy.
Extend: write a paragraph on blood imagery across 2.2 and 3.4.
Stretch: write a paragraph on how the relationship between Macbeth and his wife changes.
exit: Name one blood image.
How does Lady Macbeth react in 2.2?
Big question: how does guilt change the couple?

keywords.def: cruel and unjust use of power
the belief that life has no meaning
bringing back an earlier order
a ghostly appearance
nature that mirrors human feelings

Name one example of blood imagery.
Who is Macduff and why does he matter?

teach.heading: The slide into tyranny
bullets: 4.1: the witches' apparitions give false comfort
Macbeth decides to act first and think later
4.2: Lady Macduff and her children are killed
4.3: Macduff and Malcolm raise an army
teach.note: Summarise Act 4: Macbeth returns to the witches (4.1), receives apparitions that seem to promise safety, and then orders a massacre of Macduff's family (4.2). Explain the contrast with the English king Edward, who is a good ruler (4.3). Context: James I claimed descent from Banquo and admired Edward the Confessor's piety; be careful not to overclaim. Ask: how does Shakespeare use the killing of the innocent to show tyranny?

teach.heading: Lady Macbeth's collapse
teach.note: Read the 5.1 extract aloud. Link it to 2.2: the woman who said 'A little water clears us' now cannot wash her hands. Ask pupils to annotate the contrast. Cite 5.1.

quote.text: Out, damned spot! Out, I say!

teach.heading: Model: the 'Tomorrow' speech
teach.note: I do. Read the speech aloud. Ask pupils how it feels to hear it after learning that the queen is dead. Explain that the repeated 'tomorrow' and the stage metaphor show his despair. Cite 5.5.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's despair in 5.5?
steps: Point: he presents Macbeth as empty and hopeless.
Evidence: 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, / Creeps in this petty pace from day to day'.
Zoom: the repeated 'tomorrow' and the slow verb 'creeps' make time drag; 'petty' makes life seem small and meaningless.
Link: this contrasts with the energetic ambition of Act 1.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents Macbeth as empty and hopeless in 5.5. The repetition of 'tomorrow' and the slow verb 'creeps' make time seem to drag, while 'petty' reduces life to something small and meaningless. This despair contrasts sharply with the energetic ambition he showed in Act 1, which makes his fall seem all the more tragic.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Discuss B: this phrase shows that Macbeth has lost all sense of purpose. The common error is A, ignoring tone.

check.q: What is the best reading of Macbeth's 'Tomorrow' speech?
options: He is excited about the future.
He feels life has become meaningless and empty.
He plans to run away.
He is thinking about the witches.
check.why: B fits the slow, repetitive language. A is the opposite; C and D are not supported.

teach.heading: Downfall and order restored
bullets: 5.8: Macduff, 'untimely ripped', confronts Macbeth
Macbeth dies; Malcolm is hailed king
Malcolm calls Macbeth a 'dead butcher'
Order returns: but at what cost?
teach.note: Cite 5.8 for the duel. Explain Macduff's birth by caesarean ('untimely ripped') as the way the prophecy about men 'of woman born' is fulfilled. Ask: is Macbeth's last stand heroic? Discuss that he fights bravely at the end, so the audience feels some pity. Malcolm's closing speech restores order and legitimate kingship. Edition numbering of the last scenes differs, so check the class copy.

bullets: 30 marks, about 45 minutes
Open book: use your tabs
AO1: knowledge and response
AO2: language, form, structure; AO4: context
teach.note: Explain the task: one question from two. Example original question: 'Explore how Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition in Macbeth.' Check the latest past papers for the real stem structure; the 2025 examiner reports may help. Spend two minutes choosing, five planning. Show how a plan uses the beginning, middle and end of the play.

teach.heading: A plan grid
teach.note: Use the table to build a plan. Pupils add a short quotation and an act.scene reference for each row. Show how each row links to the question.

teach.heading: Model: a developed paragraph
teach.note: I do. Read the paragraph aloud and label each component. Show how the context is placed within the analysis. Remind pupils that all quotations are checked against the open copy.

model.problem: Explore how Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition in Macbeth.
steps: Point: ambition leads Macbeth to guilt and isolation.
Evidence: he sees the murder as so terrible that 'the multitudinous seas' will turn red (2.2).
Zoom: the vast image shows guilt too large to wash away.
Context: for a Jacobean audience, killing a king broke divine order, so guilt would feel both personal and cosmic.
Link: by 5.5, his 'Tomorrow' speech shows a man emptied by what he has done.
model.answer: Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition as guilt that cannot be cleansed. After the murder, Macbeth imagines his hand turning 'The multitudinous seas incarnadine' (2.2), a vast image suggesting guilt too large to wash away. For a Jacobean audience, killing a king broke the divine order, so this guilt would feel both personal and cosmic. By 5.5, his 'Tomorrow' speech shows a man emptied by what he has done.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Rank the responses. B is strongest because it links evidence, analysis and context. D is plot only.

check.q: Which is the best topic sentence?
options: Macbeth kills the king in Act 2.
Shakespeare shows that ambition without conscience brings isolation and despair.
Ambition is a theme.
Lady Macbeth is a woman.
check.why: B is an argument; A and D are plot or fact; C is a label with no claim.

teach.heading: Final checklist
bullets: A clear argument from the start
Short evidence with act.scene references
Analysis of words, images and structure
Context linked to Shakespeare's choices
teach.note: Pupils self-assess against the list. If time allows, they swap paragraphs and give two stars and a wish. Remind them that open-book use is a skill: they must find evidence quickly, so they should practise tabbing. Component 3 candidates will draft a similar response over time, so the planning grid still applies.
